questions.statement: The documents ___ every morning by the administration office.
questions.context: The present simple passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The subject is the thing that receives the action, so the present simple passive is are plus participle.
A bare base form would leave the verb without an auxiliary, and the sentence needs a passive structure.
Is builds the singular, and the plural subject documents requires are.
A past passive would place the checking in the past, and every morning describes a routine.

questions.explanation:
In the present simple passive the auxiliary is am, is or are and it agrees with the subject. The main verb always appears as a past participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The bridge ___ two years ago.
questions.context: The past simple passive.

options.feedback: Correct! A past passive uses was or were plus the past participle.
A present perfect would link the repair to now, but two years ago closes the action in the past.
A present continuous would place the repair under way now, which the past time denies.
A bare participle would be the past simple only in the active, and the subject is not the one repairing.

questions.explanation:
The past simple passive takes was or were plus past participle. The agent is normally introduced by by, though it is often left out when it is obvious.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: While the road ___ , a heavy lorry arrived.
questions.context: The past continuous passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The past continuous passive is was or were plus being plus participle.
That would present the repair as a single completed event with no sense of it being under way.
A present perfect would place the repair inside the present period, which the past scene denies.
A present continuous would place the repair now, and the whole scene is in the past.

questions.explanation:
Continuous passives are built with be plus being plus participle. A past continuous situation therefore needs was being plus the participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The classroom ___ at the moment. Students are arriving.
questions.context: The present continuous passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The present continuous passive is is or are plus being plus participle.
A present perfect would suggest the cleaning is already finished, but at the moment shows it is under way.
A past passive would place the cleaning in a completed past, and the sentence is about now.
A present simple passive would describe a routine, and at the moment asks about a specific action in progress.

questions.explanation:
The present continuous passive describes an action happening right now. The time expression at the moment is the clearest possible signal for the continuous form.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The results ___ tomorrow morning.
questions.context: The future simple passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The future passive uses will plus be plus past participle.
That is the active form, which would make the results the ones doing the publishing.
A present passive would need a routine or a timetable in the present.
A present perfect passive would suggest they are already out, and tomorrow is still ahead.

questions.explanation:
Future passives are simple to build: will be plus the participle. The subject of the future passive is always the thing affected.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The sample ___ before the results are announced.
questions.context: The negative form of a passive.

options.feedback: Correct! A modal plus be plus participle builds the passive in the negative.
The main verb must be a past participle, and identify in the base form is wrong.
A passive cannot be built with the auxiliary do, which carries active tenses.
A past passive would place the identification in the past, and the sentence is about the future.

questions.explanation:
Modal passives follow a fixed order: modal plus be plus past participle. The modal never changes and the participle never changes.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The tickets ___ before the departure.
questions.context: The subject of the passive is plural.

options.feedback: Correct! A past passive with a plural subject takes were plus participle.
Was builds the singular, and the subject tickets is plural.
A present continuous would place the printing now, and the tickets are printed before departure.
A bare participle would be the active past simple, with the tickets doing the printing.

questions.explanation:
Agreement in the passive depends on the subject, not on the agent. Whenever the subject is plural, the auxiliary is are, were, have been or will be.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ the application ___ yet?
questions.context: The present perfect passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The present perfect passive is have or has plus been plus participle, and yet is a present perfect marker.
That is the active form, and in the active the receiver cannot be the subject of the sentence.
The present perfect continuous passive would be have plus been being plus participle, which is not used here.
Did cannot build a perfect structure, and the question is about the present state.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect passive is used when the present state of the thing affected matters. Yet and already belong naturally to this tense.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The mural ___ by a group of local artists last year.
questions.context: The agent is named in a passive sentence.

options.feedback: Correct! A past passive with an agent introduced by by is the standard structure.
A bare participle would put the artists in the subject position, and they are not painting.
A present perfect would place the painting inside the present period, and last year closes it.
A present continuous would mean the mural is painting itself, which is not a possible reading.

questions.explanation:
By introduces the agent of a passive. It is used when the agent is worth mentioning and omitted when the action or the doer is obvious.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ the fee ___ in two instalments?
questions.context: A question in the present simple passive.

options.feedback: Correct! A polar question in the present passive takes the auxiliary is before the subject and the participle after.
Do builds active questions, and a passive question needs the be auxiliary.
A continuous passive would need being, and the fee is a payment made in one action.
A past passive would refer to a completed payment, and the question is about the general arrangement.

questions.explanation:
In a passive question the auxiliary comes before the subject and the participle closes the structure. The whole pattern mirrors the affirmative.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The teacher praised the student because she ___ a good report.
questions.context: Choosing between an active and a passive structure.

options.feedback: Correct! The active is natural here, and the past perfect shows the report was finished before the praise.
A would would build a conditional, and the praise is a statement about what really happened.
A present perfect would place the writing inside the present period, and the praise is in the past.
A present continuous would mean the report is still being written, which the praise denies.

questions.explanation:
The teacher is the natural subject of a compliment, so the active is better here. The passive is used when the doer is unknown or unimportant.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: By the time the police arrived, the stolen bikes ___ already recovered.
questions.context: The past perfect passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The past perfect passive is had plus been plus past participle.
A past simple passive would leave the two past events without a clear order.
A present perfect would measure up to now, and the police arriving is the past reference point.
Had alone would need the participle after be, and the be is what is missing here.

questions.explanation:
The past perfect passive is the passive counterpart of the past perfect. It is formed with had plus been plus the participle, exactly as it is with had plus participle in the active.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: By June the new wing ___ completely by then.
questions.context: The future perfect passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The future perfect passive is will plus have plus been plus participle.
That is the active form, and the subject would have to be the one doing the finishing.
A future simple would place the completion at the deadline without the backward view the by clause needs.
A past perfect would look back from a past point, and June is still ahead.

questions.explanation:
By plus a future deadline requires the future perfect. In the passive this becomes will have been plus the participle, which is one word longer than the active.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The results ___ when the fire alarm went off.
questions.context: The past continuous passive in a longer narrative.

options.feedback: Correct! A past continuous passive takes were plus being plus participle.
A past simple passive would present the announcement as a single finished event.
A present perfect would link the announcement to now, and the scene is in the past.
A present continuous would place the announcement now, which the alarm interrupts in the past.

questions.explanation:
An action under way at a past moment takes the past continuous passive. The being is what distinguishes this from a completed past passive.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The hall ___ for the party, but the manager refused.
questions.context: A passive with a modal in the past.

options.feedback: Correct! The past of can is could, so the modal passive is could be plus participle.
Can would place the possibility in the present, but the refusal is in the past.
Would would build a conditional, and the sentence reports a past situation.
Must would express an obligation, which is different from the possibility that was denied.

questions.explanation:
Modal passives keep the modal in front of be. The only change is the modal's own form, so can becomes could and will becomes would.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Each application ___ by two teachers and then by the director.
questions.context: The subject of the passive is the one doing the receiving.

options.feedback: Correct! Each is singular, so the present simple passive takes is plus participle.
Are would be correct for a plural subject, but each counts as singular in English.
A continuous would suggest the applications check themselves, which is impossible.
A present perfect would mean the applications do the checking, which reverses the roles.

questions.explanation:
Each, every, one and none are grammatically singular even when they look like plurals. A passive with each as its subject always takes is or was.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: This time tomorrow the documents ___ by the new system.
questions.context: The future continuous passive.

options.feedback: Correct! The future continuous passive is will plus be plus being plus participle.
A future simple would place the processing at the moment rather than showing it under way.
A present continuous would place the processing now, and this time tomorrow is still ahead.
A future perfect would look back from the future point, and the process is still running at it.

questions.explanation:
The future continuous passive is a three-part structure: will, be, being and then the participle. It is uncommon in speech but perfectly correct in formal description.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Someone has scratched the door. The door ___ during the night.
questions.context: Choosing the passive because the agent is unknown.

options.feedback: Correct! The passive is right because the person responsible is deliberately unknown.
The active would make the door the agent of scratching, which is not the meaning.
The active present perfect would also make the door the agent.
A continuous would suggest the door is acting on its own, and during the night is a closed period.

questions.explanation:
English uses the passive for two main reasons: the doer is unknown or unimportant, and the action matters more than the person who did it. Cracked doors in crime reports are the classic case.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The new law ___ by the president last Monday.
questions.context: The subject is a thing that cannot do the action, so the passive is forced.

options.feedback: Correct! A law is signed rather than signing, so the passive is the only possible structure.
The active would claim that the law itself signed itself, which is not a possible reading.
The active present perfect would have the same impossible meaning.
A past continuous would also make the law the agent of the action.

questions.explanation:
Some subjects cannot perform the action, and those verbs are almost always passive. A law is signed, a decision is taken, a prize is awarded.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "The repairs will be finished on Friday," he said. He said that the repairs ___ be finished on Friday.
questions.context: A passive in reported speech, where the auxiliary shifts.

options.feedback: Correct! In a reported passive, the first auxiliary shifts from will to would, while be finished is untouched.
Keeping will would ignore the past tense of the reporting verb he said.
Are would introduce a present passive, and the report is about a future event.
A past perfect would shift twice, and the original will needs only one step back.

questions.explanation: Backshift in a passive sentence affects the first auxiliary only. Will be finished becomes would be finished, and the passive part of the verb never changes.
questions.subject: ingles
